title: YOU CALL YOURSELF A CHRISTIAN… BUT WOULD JESUS RECOGNIZE THE LIFE YOU’RE LIVING?
paragraphs: YOU CALL YOURSELF A CHRISTIAN… BUT WOULD JESUS RECOGNIZE THE LIFE YOU’RE LIVING?
The Most Terrifying Thing Isn't That the World Might Discover Who You Really Are. It's That You Could Spend Your Whole Life Calling Jesus “Lord”… Without Ever Truly Surrendering to Him.
Not because it was spoken to atheists.
Not because it was directed at people who openly hated God.
But because Jesus spoke it about people who called Him Lord.
People who believed they belonged to Him.
People who even pointed to extraordinary religious works as evidence of their relationship with Him.
And when the moment came for them to stand before Him, they heard words no human soul should ever want to hear.
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23, KJV
Read that again.
Not, “I knew you once, but forgot you.”
Not, “You didn't attend enough church services.”
Not, “You didn't donate enough money.”
“I never knew you.”
Imagine spending decades speaking His name, posting Bible verses, attending worship services, defending Christianity in arguments, and telling everyone you believe in God…
Only to discover that the faith you displayed publicly was never the surrender Jesus called for privately.
And before you dismiss this as another message about hypocrites, there is something you need to understand.
The most dangerous spiritual deception is not always believing there is no God.
Sometimes it is believing you belong to God while refusing to let Him rule your life.
And the frightening part?
You can become so comfortable with that contradiction that eventually, you stop noticing it.
You know how to raise your hands during worship.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know which Bible verses to post when life becomes difficult.
You know how to look spiritually strong when someone asks how you're doing.
But there are things nobody sees.
The bitterness you've been feeding.
The forgiveness you've been postponing.
The secret habits you've been defending.
The person you keep hurting while insisting you're a good Christian.
The truth you keep avoiding because obedience might cost you something.
And somewhere between Sunday worship and Monday morning, a question quietly waits for you.
If someone removed the Christian label from your life, would the way you live still point them to Jesus?
Not perfectly.
Not flawlessly.
But genuinely.
Would they recognize His love in how you treat people who cannot benefit you?
His mercy in how you respond when someone fails?
His truth in what you do when lying would be easier?
His humility in how you behave when nobody applauds?
His holiness in what you choose when nobody is watching?
Because Christianity was never meant to be a costume we put on when people are looking.
It is a new life received through Jesus Christ.
And sometimes the hardest person to confront with that truth is the one looking back at us in the mirror.
There is something remarkable about the original Greek of Matthew 7:23.
Jesus says:
“Οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς.”
Oudepote egnōn hymas.
“I never knew you.”
The word ἔγνων (egnōn) comes from γινώσκω (ginōskō), meaning “to know.”
In this context, Jesus is not suggesting He lacked information about these people. Scripture presents Him as the One who knows what is in the human heart (John 2:24–25).
The issue is not whether Jesus possessed knowledge of their existence.
The issue is whether they truly belonged to Him.
That distinction should shake us.
You can know facts about Jesus without knowing Jesus.
You can memorize His teachings while resisting His authority.
You can admire His compassion while refusing to show compassion.
You can speak passionately about the cross while refusing to surrender the sins He died to redeem you from.
And you can become so skilled at looking like a Christian that you forget to ask whether you are actually following Christ.
But there is another side to this warning, and you need to hear it before fear convinces you to run away.
Jesus did not speak these words so that every struggling believer would live in constant terror of rejection.
He spoke them as a warning against false confidence, empty profession, and a life that claims His name while practicing lawlessness.
The Christian who hates their sin, grieves over their failures, and keeps returning to Christ in repentance is not the same as the person who has made peace with rebellion.
There is a difference between falling into sin and deciding that sin will remain your master.
There is a difference between struggling to obey Jesus and having no intention of obeying Him.
There is a difference between a wounded sheep who needs the Shepherd and a religious performer who believes the costume is enough.
And perhaps that distinction is exactly what someone reading this desperately needs today.
Because you may be sitting there thinking…
I've failed too many times.
I've made promises to God that I didn't keep.
I've prayed for forgiveness and then found myself struggling with the same temptation again.
What if I'm one of the people Jesus is talking about?
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to pretend your sin is harmless.
But neither is the answer to conclude that Christ's mercy has run out.
The same Jesus who warns against false discipleship also invites weary sinners to come to Him.
He said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
Do not let the enemy use a warning intended to awaken your conscience as an excuse to keep you away from the Savior.
Run toward Christ.
Not away from Him.
Because the purpose of conviction is not merely to make you feel terrible about yourself.
It is to bring you to the One who can forgive, cleanse, and transform you.
And perhaps no story reveals this more powerfully than the night one of Jesus' closest disciples discovered just how weak his own confidence really was.
His name was Peter.
Peter wasn't an outsider.
He wasn't someone who had never heard Jesus preach.
He had walked with Him.
Watched miracles unfold.
Heard the voice that commanded storms.
Seen the glory of Christ revealed.
And when Jesus warned that His disciples would stumble, Peter was convinced that his devotion was stronger than everyone else's.
He said:
“Though all men shall be offended because of thee, yet will I never be offended.” — Matthew 26:33, KJV
In other words…
Other people might abandon You, Lord.
But not me.
I'm different.
I'm loyal.
I'm stronger than that.
How many of us have said something similar?
Maybe not aloud.
But in our hearts.
I would never cheat.
I would never betray someone.
I would never become addicted.
I would never walk away from God.
I would never be like those hypocritical Christians.
Until the day temptation arrived wearing a face we recognized.
Until loneliness made compromise seem comforting.
Until anger became stronger than restraint.
Until fear made honesty feel dangerous.
Until the person we thought we were collided with the person our choices revealed.
That night, Peter denied Jesus.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
And Luke records one detail that makes the entire scene almost unbearable.
“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.” — Luke 22:61, KJV
Imagine that moment.
The courtyard.
The accusations.
The fear.
The words Peter had just spoken.
And then…
Jesus looked at him.
Scripture does not describe the exact expression on Jesus' face, so we should not pretend to know what Peter saw in His eyes.
But we do know what happened next.
Peter remembered the Lord's warning.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
The man who had confidently declared that he would never abandon Jesus had just discovered the weakness of his own heart.
His public confidence had collapsed under private fear.
And maybe you understand that kind of collapse.
Maybe you remember the moment you realized you were capable of something you once condemned in others.
Maybe you remember sitting alone after an argument, knowing your words had wounded someone you loved.
Maybe you remember deleting messages, hiding evidence, or rehearsing explanations because you were terrified of being exposed.
Maybe you remember the moment after giving in to temptation when the pleasure disappeared and shame remained.
And perhaps the most painful thought wasn't simply, What have I done?
It was…
How could I call myself a Christian and still do this?
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
That is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
After His crucifixion and resurrection, Jesus did not erase Peter from the story.
In John 21, the risen Christ met His disciples by the Sea of Tiberias.
There, Jesus asked Peter three times whether he loved Him.
And He entrusted Peter with the responsibility to care for His sheep.
The man who had denied Jesus three times was not restored by pretending his denial never happened.
He was restored through an encounter with the risen Savior who knew the truth about him.
Peter's failure was real.
His grief was real.
And Christ's grace was real.
Jesus did not call Peter's betrayal good. He proved that betrayal did not have to be the final chapter of Peter's life.
That is what grace does.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace brings sinners out of darkness.
Grace does not tell you that repentance is unnecessary.
Grace makes repentance possible.
Grace does not teach you to become comfortable with the chains that are destroying you.
Grace leads you to the Savior who breaks their power.
And this is where the message becomes painfully personal.
Because many people want Jesus as their Rescuer while resisting Him as their Lord.
We want Him to calm our anxiety, but we resist His command to trust Him.
We want Him to forgive our sins, but we struggle to forgive those who have sinned against us.
We want Him to bless our relationships, but we refuse to surrender relationships built on deception.
We want Him to heal our hearts, but we keep reopening wounds through bitterness.
We want the comfort of His promises without the inconvenience of His commands.
We want resurrection power without putting the old life to death.
And yet Jesus never presented discipleship as an arrangement where we could keep our old masters and simply add His name to the list.
He said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” — Luke 9:23, KJV
Daily.
Not just when the worship music is playing.
Not just when life is falling apart.
Not just when someone needs prayer.
Daily.
When you're tired.
When you're misunderstood.
When nobody appreciates your sacrifice.
When temptation whispers that one more compromise won't matter.
When forgiveness feels unfair.
When doing what is right costs you comfort, approval, opportunity, or pride.
Following Jesus means learning to say no to the version of ourselves that insists on being its own god.
But please understand something essential.
We do not become Christians by successfully performing enough acts of obedience.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
And the very next verse tells us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The order matters.
Good works are not the price we pay to purchase salvation. They are the fruit of a life being transformed by the Savior.
A tree does not become alive by attaching fruit to its branches.
A living tree produces fruit because life is already at work within it.
That is why Jesus said:
“Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.” — Matthew 7:20, KJV
He did not say that genuine believers would never struggle.
He did not say that every Christian would mature at the same pace.
He did not say that a single failure automatically proves a person never knew Him.
But He did teach that what grows from our lives matters.
So perhaps the question is not simply whether you have a Christian identity.
Perhaps it is whether your life increasingly bears evidence of Christ's transforming work.
Are you becoming more truthful?
More willing to repent?
More compassionate toward the wounded?
More willing to forgive?
More sensitive to sin?
More hungry for Scripture?
More dependent on prayer?
More concerned with pleasing God than impressing people?
And when you fail, do you return to Christ in humble repentance, or do you continually search for excuses to protect the sin you refuse to surrender?
This is not about achieving perfection before God will love you.
It is about whether the grace you profess is teaching you to walk in a new direction.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.” — 2 Corinthians 13:5, KJV
The original Greek begins:
“Ἑαυτοὺς πειράζετε εἰ ἐστὲ ἐν τῇ πίστει.”
Heautous peirazete ei este en tē pistei.
“Examine yourselves, whether you are in the faith.”
The verb πειράζετε (peirazete) here carries the sense of testing or examining.
Paul is calling for honest spiritual self-examination, not endless self-torment.
Because there is a kind of self-examination that leads us to Christ.
And there is a kind of self-obsession that keeps our eyes fixed on our failures instead of His sufficiency.
The purpose is not to become consumed with the question, Am I good enough?
The answer to that question, apart from Christ, is no.
The better question is…
Am I truly trusting the Jesus who is enough, and is His grace changing the way I live?
That question reaches beyond religious appearances.
It reaches the person who is admired in church but feared at home.
The person who quotes Scripture online but humiliates strangers in comment sections.
The person who publicly celebrates God's mercy but privately refuses to extend mercy.
The person who speaks about holiness while protecting a hidden pattern of exploitation.
The person who calls for repentance in everyone else but becomes furious when someone lovingly confronts their own sin.
And yes, it reaches the person writing this message as much as the person reading it.
Nobody gets to stand above the Word of God.
We all stand beneath its authority.
We all need grace.
We all need the Savior.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that some of us are morally impressive enough to deserve heaven.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
The apostle Paul, who once persecuted the church, wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” — 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
Consider who said that.
A man who had once approved of violence against followers of Jesus.
A man whose past was stained with persecution.
A man who could never honestly rewrite his history to make himself look innocent.
And yet that same man became a witness to the mercy of Christ.
Paul did not glorify his former sin.
He glorified the Savior who showed him mercy.
That is the difference between a testimony and an excuse.
A testimony says, Look what Jesus rescued me from.
An excuse says, Because Jesus forgives, I don't need to change.
The first magnifies grace.
The second distorts it.
And Scripture will not allow us to confuse the two.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts the idea that grace gives us permission to continue comfortably in sin.
Paul's answer is unmistakable:
“God forbid.”
Grace is not a license to remain enslaved.
Grace is the gift that brings us into a new relationship with God through Jesus Christ.
And sometimes that transformation begins in the least glamorous places imaginable.
It begins when you apologize without adding an excuse.
When you finally confess what you've been hiding.
When you stop feeding the conversation that is pulling you toward adultery.
When you choose not to retaliate against someone who embarrassed you.
When you return what you dishonestly took.
When you admit you need help.
When you seek accountability instead of pretending you can fight every temptation alone.
When you open the Bible not to find a verse that justifies your anger, but to hear what God actually says.
When you kneel beside your bed and whisper a prayer nobody else will ever hear.
Lord, I cannot keep living like this.
I have called You Lord while fighting to remain in control.
I have wanted Your forgiveness without surrendering what is destroying me.
Please change my heart.
And perhaps the tears come.
Perhaps they don't.
Real repentance is not measured by how dramatically someone cries.
It is a turning of the heart toward God that bears fruit in a changed direction.
The Hebrew Scriptures give us a beautiful word that helps illuminate this.
שׁוּב — shuv
It means “to turn” or “to return,” and in many Old Testament passages it describes turning back to God.
Listen to the invitation in Joel 2:12:
“Turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.” — KJV
The Hebrew begins:
“שֻׁבוּ עָדַי בְּכָל־לְבַבְכֶם”
Shuvu ʿadai bekhol-levavkhem.
“Return to me with all your heart.”
And in Joel 2:13, the prophet calls the people to rend their hearts and not merely their garments.
That image matters.
In the ancient world, tearing one's garments could express grief or distress.
But God was calling His people beyond outward displays.
He wanted hearts genuinely turned toward Him.
Not religious theater.
Not public performances of sorrow.
Not dramatic words designed to impress an audience.
The heart.
The place where motives hide.
The place where loyalties are revealed.
The place where surrender must become real.
And perhaps that is what Jesus is confronting in your life today.
Not the fact that you have ever failed.
But the fact that you have become skilled at disguising the places where you refuse to yield.
You can fool an audience.
You can fool your family.
You can fool your church friends.
You can even deceive yourself for a season.
But you cannot manufacture a relationship with Christ through appearances.
And that is not meant to leave you hopeless.
It is meant to invite you into honesty.
Because the One who knows the truth about you is also the One who went to the cross for sinners.
Think about that.
Jesus did not enter the world because humanity needed better religious branding.
He came because we needed redemption.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again, according to the Scriptures.
The cross reveals how seriously God takes sin.
The resurrection declares the victory of Jesus Christ over death.
And the Gospel calls us to repent and believe in Him.
Not merely to admire Him.
Not merely to quote Him.
Not merely to wear His name.
To trust Him.
To follow Him.
To belong to Him.
And that means your past, however ugly, does not have to be your future.
The liar can become truthful.
The proud can learn humility.
The bitter can learn forgiveness.
The addicted can seek help, walk in accountability, and experience real change.
The unfaithful can repent and begin the difficult work of rebuilding integrity, even when consequences remain.
The religious hypocrite can stop performing and begin living honestly before God.
Not because human willpower is unlimited.
But because the Holy Spirit is at work in those who belong to Christ.
And that work is often a process.
Some battles are long.
Some wounds require time, prayer, wise counsel, and patient care.
Some consequences do not disappear simply because forgiveness has been received.
But none of that means Jesus has abandoned the believer who continues turning toward Him.
Philippians 1:6 reminds us that the God who begins a good work in His people will bring it to completion.
He is not finished shaping His children.
And there is a remarkable promise in Ezekiel 36:26:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.” — KJV
Notice what God promises.
Not merely a better reputation.
Not merely improved religious habits.
A new heart.
That is the miracle we need.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about teaching a dead heart to imitate life.
It is about God's power to give new life.
And perhaps, after all these words, the most important question is no longer whether Jesus would recognize the Christian image you've built.
The deeper question is whether you will stop hiding behind that image and come honestly to Him.
Maybe you have been pretending for years.
Maybe you've drifted slowly.
Not through one dramatic decision.
But through a thousand small compromises.
A prayer neglected.
A conviction ignored.
An apology postponed.
A sin justified.
A warning dismissed.
Until one day, the things that once grieved you barely trouble your conscience anymore.
And you cannot remember when your relationship with Jesus became more about maintaining appearances than walking with Him.
If that is you, please hear this.
You do not have to continue pretending.
You can repent today.
You can confess your sins to God today.
You can ask forgiveness from the people you've wronged.
You can seek help for the patterns you've been unable to overcome alone.
You can return to Scripture.
You can begin praying again.
You can stop defending the very things Christ is calling you to surrender.
And if you've never truly placed your faith in Jesus Christ, you can turn to Him now.
You do not need to manufacture a flawless past before coming to the Savior.
You need His mercy.
And His invitation is not reserved for people with impressive spiritual résumés.
It is extended to sinners who come to Him in faith.
Remember the criminal crucified beside Jesus.
He had no opportunity to build a long history of Christian service.
No opportunity to establish a public ministry.
No opportunity to repair every earthly consequence of his crimes.
But he turned to Jesus in faith.
And Jesus said:
“To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43, KJV
Salvation was not purchased by the man's religious accomplishments.
His hope rested in Christ.
And the same Gospel that offered hope to a dying criminal still calls sinners to repentance and faith today.
So please do not misunderstand this message.
Jesus Christ is the Savior. No ministry can sell what His grace freely gives.
It is also not saying that every genuine Christian must display the same level of maturity.
A new believer learning to walk with Jesus and a mature believer who has followed Him for decades may be at very different stages.
But both need the same Savior.
Both depend on grace.
Both are called to follow Him.
And both must remember that faith is not merely a word on a profile.
It is trust in the living Christ.
Now, before you leave this article, I want to ask you something.
Not as an accusation.
Not as a demand for public confession.
But as an invitation to be honest before God.
What is the one area of your life where you know Jesus is calling you to stop pretending and start surrendering?
Maybe it is your anger.
Your pride.
Your marriage.
Your secret habits.
Your unforgiveness.
Your dishonesty.
Your fear of what others might think.
Or perhaps it is simply that you have been trying to look strong for so long that you have forgotten how to admit you need help.
You do not have to reveal private details that could harm you or someone else.
Not because commenting earns God's approval.
Not because a public declaration automatically proves repentance.
But because sometimes an honest sentence becomes the beginning of a conversation, a prayer, or a connection with another believer who reminds us that we do not have to walk alone.
Not to collect another inspirational post.
For the evening when pride tells you that you don't need to apologize.
For the day when shame whispers that your failure is greater than Christ's mercy.
Return to the Scriptures quoted here.
Read their surrounding passages.
Ask God to teach you not merely to feel convicted for a moment, but to walk faithfully with Him.
And think about one person who might need this message.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to attack.
Someone you love.
Someone who has quietly drifted from faith.
Someone who believes their mistakes have placed them beyond forgiveness.
Someone who attends church but feels spiritually empty.
Someone who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy and needs to see the difference between human failure and the character of Jesus Christ.
Or send this privately with a simple message:
I thought of you while reading this. I hope it reminds you how much Jesus still matters.
One thoughtful share can carry Scripture into the life of someone who may never visit a church page, open a devotional, or search for a sermon.
You may never know who reads it quietly.
Who pauses halfway through.
Who opens their Bible afterward.
Who finally asks for prayer.
Who decides to return to church.
Who begins seeking Jesus again.
The outcome belongs to God.
But sharing the truth with love is one simple way we can serve others.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following around a personality.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to turn conviction into a business.
But to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, biblical teaching, encouragement, repentance, healing, and practical discipleship.
There are people who need more than another passing motivational quote.
They need biblical truth.
They need patient encouragement.
They need to understand the Gospel.
They need to know that holiness matters, repentance matters, and grace is real.
Resources to help you study Scripture.
Strengthen your understanding of the Christian faith.
Develop a more consistent devotional life.
Grow in prayer.
And continue learning what it means to follow Jesus beyond the emotional moment of a single article.
We want those resources to continue reaching people who are hungry for God's Word.
And we want to keep expanding that work.
God is glorified through faith in Christ and lives of love, obedience, worship, and generosity.
And when believers freely choose to support trustworthy Gospel-centered work, that generosity can become one expression of their desire to serve others for His glory.
These products can be everyday reminders of faith, thoughtful gifts, or useful resources for personal growth.
It is the opportunity to help keep biblical encouragement and discipleship resources available to people who need them.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, comment, and use the free resources.
Your value before God is not determined by what you can afford to give.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And genuine Christian generosity must remain willing, not coerced.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, giving is to be done according to what one has decided in the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the hero of this story.
Jesus is.
And that brings us back to the question that began everything.
You call yourself a Christian… but would Jesus recognize the life you're living?
Perhaps, after reading this, you are afraid of what the answer might reveal.
But don't end here staring at your failures.
Look to Christ.
The One who warned about empty religion is the same One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who exposed hypocrisy is the same One who restored Peter.
The One who commanded us to follow Him is the same One who laid down His life for His sheep.
And the One who calls us to repentance is the same One whose resurrection gives us hope for a genuinely new life.
Do not mistake His patience for permission to remain unchanged.
But do not mistake His holiness for an unwillingness to forgive.
Come to Him.
Tell Him the truth.
Turn from the sin you've been defending.
Trust in His finished work.
Ask the Holy Spirit to transform what you cannot repair through appearances or willpower.
And when you stumble, do not build a home in your failure.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Get up.
Follow Him again.
Not to earn the cross.
But because of what Jesus accomplished there.
If you need words to begin, you can pray something like this:

Lord Jesus, You know the person I show the world, and You know the person I am when nobody is watching. You know my sins, my excuses, my fears, and the things I have tried to hide. I cannot save myself through religious appearances or good works. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I turn to You for forgiveness and new life. Teach me to repent sincerely, trust Your grace, obey Your Word, and love others as You have loved me. Change the desires I keep protecting. Heal what is wounded. Expose what is false. Strengthen what is weak. And let my life increasingly reflect the truth that I belong to You. Amen.
The prayer itself is not a magic formula.
Its words cannot replace genuine faith.
But the Savior to whom it is directed is real.
And His mercy is greater than the religious image you have been trying so desperately to maintain.
One day, the applause will stop.
The notifications will disappear.
The religious titles will mean nothing.
The carefully managed image will no longer be able to speak for you.
And what will matter is not how convincingly you performed Christianity before the world.
What will matter is whether you truly belong to Jesus Christ.
So don't spend your life polishing a Christian image while neglecting the Savior who came to give you a new heart.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be that people discovered you were a sinner. It would be that you spent your life hiding from the only Savior who could redeem you.
